passage: The pouring rain kept everyone in the school hall, and only one football and one skipping rope were left. Samir wanted football, and Francis wanted skipping. They stood facing each other, arms folded. The bell would ring in ten minutes. Samir said, “What if you pick this one, and I pick the next?” Francis frowned. “Skipping first?” “Skipping first,” Samir said. “Then football after lunch.” Francis thought about it. “Okay, but you remember.” “I'll write it on my hand.” Samir scribbled “football after lunch” on his palm. Francis grinned and picked up the rope.

qa.q: What did Samir write on his palm?
qa.a: “Football after lunch.”

qa.q: How was Francis feeling when he first stood with folded arms, and what changed?
qa.a: Francis was resisting and wanted skipping, but hearing a fair trade made Francis willing to agree.

qa.q: Why did the compromise work for both children?
qa.a: Each got a turn, Francis was heard first, and Samir wrote the deal on his hand so it would be remembered.

qa.q: How might Samir have felt giving up his pick for the first turn?
qa.a: He may have felt a little disappointed but comfortable, since he knew his football turn was coming.

grounding: A child proposes turns, you pick this game and I pick the next, and compromise works when both feel heard and the deal is remembered.

passage: “You pick the game today, I pick tomorrow,” Anand told Disha in the living room, holding the two board games. Disha crossed her arms. “But I always pick second.” “Then let's flip a coin,” Anand said. Disha shook her head. “Coins make me lose.” Anand thought. “Okay. You pick today. I'll pick the next two days.” Disha's face relaxed. “Two days? That's fair.” “Deal,” said Anand. They shook hands. Their mother, folding clothes nearby, smiled. Disha picked the snake game. Anand set up the pieces. “Tomorrow it's mine,” he said, and Disha nodded.

qa.q: Which game did Disha pick?
qa.a: The snake game.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she said she always picks second?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and was holding her ground, which is why she crossed her arms.

qa.q: What made Anand's second offer work?
qa.a: He listened to her reason, dropped the coin and offered her today while he took the next two days, so she felt heard.

qa.q: How might their mother see the deal?
qa.a: She may be pleased they worked it out themselves, since she watched and smiled.

grounding: A child proposes turns, splitting days and trading choices, and compromise works when both feel heard and the deal is remembered.

passage: “Ludo!” “No, hide-and-seek!” Yamini and Devika glared at each other across the veranda. “We played ludo yesterday,” said Devika. “And hide-and-seek the day before.” “Because you always want it.” Yamini folded her arms. Then she sighed. “Okay. What if you pick first today, and I pick second? Half an hour each.” Devika thought. “And tomorrow I pick second?” “Yes. We swap.” “Who keeps time?” “Your mum's clock. We can see it from here.” Devika grinned. “Hide-and-seek first. You count.” Half an hour later, Devika called, “Time! Ludo now,” before Yamini even asked.

qa.q: How long did each game get?
qa.a: Each game got half an hour.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she folded her arms?
qa.a: Yamini felt frustrated and stubborn, sure Devika always got her way.

qa.q: What made the compromise work?
qa.a: Both got a turn, they agreed to swap the order tomorrow and used the clock to keep time, so both felt heard.

qa.q: What did Devika's “Time! Ludo now” show?
qa.a: It showed Devika remembered the deal and kept it fairly, without Yamini needing to remind her.

grounding: Shows a child proposing turns, you pick this game and I pick the next, and the deal working because both feel heard and remember it.

passage: I'm Afreen. Two summers ago, my cousin Chandrika and I had to share one bicycle at Nani's house in Ranchi. For the first three days we fought every hour. She'd grab it after breakfast; I'd grab it after lunch; Nani had to hide it in the cowshed. On the fourth day, I said, “What if you have it every morning and I have it every evening, when it's cooler?” Chandrika said, “But evenings are better.” “Then we swap after one week.” We wrote the deal on the back of a calendar and stuck it by the door. When I forgot once and took it in the morning, Chandrika just pointed at the calendar. I gave it back. We didn't fight once after that.

qa.q: Where was the deal written?
qa.a: It was written on the back of a calendar stuck by the door.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she said “But evenings are better”?
qa.a: Chandrika felt the first plan was unfair and was worried about getting the worse time.

qa.q: Why did the compromise last?
qa.a: It swapped after a week so both got the better time, and writing it down helped them remember and keep the deal.

qa.q: How did Nani deal with the fighting before the deal?
qa.a: Nani had to hide the bicycle in the cowshed to stop the fights.

grounding: Shows children splitting time on a shared bicycle, a compromise that works because both are heard and the deal is remembered.

passage: Group-work note, Friday. Ms Kapoor, Class 6. Zeenat and Bhupen both wanted to present their group's project on rivers, and by Wednesday they weren't speaking. Today Zeenat came to me with a plan written on a sheet: “Bhupen does the introduction and the map. I do the dams and the conclusion. We both answer questions.” I asked if Bhupen had agreed. She said, “Not yet. I wanted to check it was fair first.” I sent her to ask him. Bhupen read it twice and added one line: “Zeenat holds the pointer for my part, I hold it for hers.” They shook on it. The presentation went smoothly, and they swapped the pointer exactly as written.

qa.q: Which parts did Zeenat take in the presentation?
qa.a: Zeenat took the dams and the conclusion.

qa.q: What was Bhupen likely feeling when he read the plan twice?
qa.a: Bhupen was likely careful and a bit wary, checking the deal was fair before agreeing.

qa.q: What made the compromise work?
qa.a: Each got fair parts, Bhupen added his own line so he felt heard, and they kept to the deal exactly as written.

qa.q: How did Ms Kapoor support the compromise?
qa.a: She checked whether Bhupen had agreed and sent Zeenat to ask him, making sure both sides were heard.

grounding: Shows a child proposing to split a shared task, with the compromise working because both sides are heard and the deal is kept.

passage:
Tuesday, after school
Today Avni and I nearly stopped being friends over hopscotch. Avni wanted hopscotch at break. I wanted to finish our chalk city on the back steps. We both stood there with our arms folded for ages, and break kept getting shorter.
Then I had an idea. I said, "Hopscotch today, chalk city tomorrow. And on Friday we toss a coin for who picks."
Avni thought about it. "Only if you write it down so you don't forget."
So I wrote it on a page from my rough book and we both signed it like a real contract. Hopscotch was actually fun. I even got to square eight.
The page is folded in my pencil box. Tomorrow is MY turn 😊
- Vidya

qa.q: Where did Vidya put the written deal?
qa.a: The page is folded in Vidya's pencil box.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling while the two friends stood with arms folded?
qa.a: Vidya felt stubborn and also worried, because break kept getting shorter and the quarrel was putting the friendship at risk.

qa.q: Why did writing the deal down help?
qa.a: It turned the promise into something both could remember and check, which was Avni's condition for agreeing, so neither would feel cheated the next day.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt about the deal?
qa.a: Avni probably felt heard and relieved that hopscotch came first, and safer saying yes once the promise was signed 🙂

grounding: It shows a child proposing a turn-taking deal to a friend and the compromise working because both felt heard and the deal was written down to be remembered.
